In other words, it is created, just like everything else in the created universe.
To say that God “speaks,” on this view, simply means that God creates speech.
This is the origin and basic meaning of the question as the Muʿtazilites understood it.
But they did not stop there.

They also tried to support their position with other arguments. Some of these aimed to show that belief in an eternal Qurʾān did not merely conflict with divine unity. It also conflicted with the rational character of Qurʾānic law.
Suppose the Qurʾān were eternal speech—that is, an eternal attribute of the eternal divine essence.
Then the commands contained in the Qurʾān would also have to be eternal.
But that would mean that God’s commands existed before the people to whom they were addressed existed.
Before human beings existed, there would have been no one for the commands to apply to.
Human beings are the subjects of these commands.
How, then, could God issue commands to people who did not yet exist?
The Muʿtazilites argued that this would be meaningless, and meaningless action cannot be attributed to God.
They also said that speech requires both someone who speaks and someone who is addressed.
Before the people subject to God’s commands existed, there would have been a speaker but no listener or addressee.
For this reason, they argued, belief in an eternal Qurʾān would make divine legislation irrational, and the claim must therefore be false.
They also approached the question from another direction.

They argued that God’s created speech exists in a particular place or medium. It consists of letters and sounds, while the written copies found in Qurʾānic manuscripts reproduce those letters and sounds. Anything that exists in a particular place is an accident, and accidents pass away immediately.
This argument returns us to the distinction between substance and accident.
The Muʿtazilites began from what they accepted as established: God is a simple substance and cannot be one of the accidents.
An accident, in their argument here, is bodily, while divinity is absolutely free from bodily form.
It exists somewhere because it consists of letters and sounds that are spoken and heard. These therefore exist in the physical organs of speech and hearing.
The Qurʾān is also written on paper. Many copies can be made, each reproducing the same text. In this sense too, it exists in a particular place.
Anything that exists in a place is an accident, and accidents pass away.
The spoken letters and sounds that make up the Qurʾān disappear as soon as they have been spoken or heard.
All of this separates them from a substance that does not exist in a place, does not take bodily form and does not pass away.
The Qurʾān therefore cannot be eternal or identical with the divine essence.
It must have come into existence and been created, like other created things.
Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, whom al-Shahrastānī calls the leading master of the Muʿtazila, gives another version of essentially the same argument.
We saw earlier that al-ʿAllāf understood God’s will as an act of creation.
When God wills something, He creates it. His will for a thing is His saying to it, “Be,” and it is.
But al-ʿAllāf distinguished between two kinds of divine will: the will that creates, and the will that imposes duties.
The first, in his view, does not exist in a particular place.
The Qurʾān belongs to this second kind because it contains duties and laws addressed to human beings: commands, prohibitions and statements about paradise and hell.
The Qurʾān is therefore legislative speech that exists in a place.
Al-ʿAllāf answers that it obviously cannot be God’s own essence.
God’s essence cannot be the place in which commands, prohibitions and reports exist.
The place must therefore be something other than God.
If the Qurʾān is speech that exists in something other than God, then it is a created accident like other accidents.
God created the Qurʾān in the Preserved Tablet. By this expression, al-ʿAllāf means the mental or immaterial existence of created things before their material existence.
The Qurʾān, he says, exists in three kinds of place: a place where it is preserved, a place where it is written, and a place where it is recited and heard.
It can exist in many places at the same time without literally being transported, moving or passing from one place to another.
But if God were to destroy all the places in which it is preserved, read or heard, the Qurʾān would cease to exist.
The logical conclusion of al-ʿAllāf’s argument is that the Qurʾān is an accident rather than a substance.
It is therefore created and came into existence in time, rather than being eternal.
Maʿmar ibn ʿAbbād al-Sulamī, whom we discussed earlier, also accepted the Muʿtazilite position that the Qurʾān was created rather than eternal.
But he differed from the other Muʿtazilites in one important respect.
He argued that the Qurʾān was not directly an act of God.
His reasoning followed from his wider theory of bodies and their properties.
The Qurʾān is something produced, and as such it is an accident. But Maʿmar held that accidents cannot literally be produced by God.
The Qurʾān must therefore be produced by the thing from which its sound is heard.
If Qurʾānic speech were heard from a tree, for example, that speech would be an act of the tree itself.
Whenever it is heard, it is the act of the thing in which it occurs.
Al-Ashʿarī explains this by saying that Maʿmar regarded the Qurʾān as an accident and believed that accidents could not be acts of God.
Al-Shahrastānī gives the same idea in another form. According to him, Maʿmar believed that God created only bodies. The properties or accidents of bodies are produced by those bodies themselves.
Some arise naturally: fire produces burning, the sun produces heat and the moon produces changes of colour.
Others arise through choice: living beings produce movement and rest, coming together and separating.
Yet Maʿmar does not deny that the Qurʾān is created by God, as al-Baghdādī tries to interpret his position.
For Maʿmar, the Qurʾān is a body, and God creates bodies.
What God does not create are the actions and temporary properties of those bodies.
This is similar to what the Muʿtazilites say about human beings and their actions.
The human being is created by God, but human actions are not. Human beings create their own acts. This is how the Muʿtazilites defend human freedom.
Once the Muʿtazilites had developed rational arguments for the created nature of the Qurʾān, they turned to the Qurʾānic text itself.
They interpreted its verses in ways that agreed with the conclusions they had already reached through reason, and they used those interpretations to support their position.
For example, they considered the verse:
“A Book whose verses were made firm and then set out in detail.” (Sūrat Hūd, verse 3)
They argued that this shows the Qurʾān to be made up of parts that appeared in stages: first made firm, then set out in detail.
That can only apply to something that comes into existence, not to something eternal.
They argued that “sending down” is clearly an event—something that happens.
What is eternal does not “come down.”
Perhaps their strongest textual argument came from the verse:
“Whenever We abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We bring one better than it.” (Sūrat al-Baqara, verse 106)
For the Muʿtazilites, abrogation means change.
And change is one of the clearest marks of something that has come into existence, as opposed to something eternal that cannot undergo any change.
Any realistic assessment of the Muʿtazilite position on the created Qurʾān—and indeed on the whole question of God’s attributes—must begin from two points.
First, the Muʿtazilites were determined to defend an idea of divine unity completely free from every form of multiplicity, even purely mental multiplicity.
Second, they were equally determined to understand divine unity rationally.

They judged religious texts in the light of reason. They did not simply ignore apparent contradictions in those texts and surrender them to unquestioning faith. When the literal meaning of a text seemed to conflict with reason, they interpreted it.
A proper study of the intellectual basis of Muʿtazilite theory in this area has to begin from these two principles.
From the same starting point, we can also examine the claim that the Muʿtazilites took these ideas from outside sources.
Some writers say that they borrowed one idea or another from the philosophers, as al-Shahrastānī suggests.
Others say they took their ideas from Jews, Christians or Persian Manichaeans, as some early historians and some Orientalists have claimed.
There is no reason to deny the relationship between later Muʿtazilite thinkers and the philosophers.
It is a historical fact, and we have no doubt about it.
Here we mean the later Muʿtazilites, beginning with al-ʿAllāf and al-Naẓẓām.
